cards.front: What are the eligibility criteria for being elected as a member of a Panchayat and how are the chairpersons of Panchayats at village, intermediate and district levels elected?
cards.back:
Qualifications:

  • Must be a citizen of India.
  • Must have attained 21 years of age.
  • Must be registered as a voter in the Panchayat area
Level Chairperson How elected
Village level Sarpanch / Pradhan (Gram Panchayat chairperson) Directly elected by the voters of the village (general rule under State Panchayat laws)
Intermediate level Chairperson of Panchayat Samiti / Block Panchayat Elected indirectly by and from among the elected members of the Panchayat at that level
District level Chairperson of Zila Parishad Elected indirectly by and from among the elected members of the Zila Parishad

cards.front: What constitutes the electoral college for the election of the President of India?
cards.back:
The electoral college for the President consists of:

  1. Elected members of both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha)
  2. Elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of States
  3. Elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of UTs of Delhi and Puducherry

Excluded (do NOT take part):

  • Nominated members of Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies
  • All members of Legislative Councils (both elected and nominated)

cards.front: What happens during zero hour and question hour. Are these terms mentioned in constitution of India.
When & how is the Committee on Official Language constituted? Who are the members and what is their main function.
cards.back:
Aspect Key points to recall
Constitution (Trigger + process) After 10 years from the date Section 3 comes into force → Committee is constituted by a resolution moved in either House, with previous sanction of the President, and passed by both Houses.
Strength & composition 30 members: 20 from Lok Sabha + 10 from Rajya Sabha.
Functions / duty Review progress in the use of Hindi for the official purposes of the Union.

cards.front: Name three important legislative powers of the President.
cards.back:
• Summons, prorogues Parliament; can dissolve Lok Sabha.
  • Gives assent to Bills; can withhold or return (except Money Bills & Constitutional Amendment Bills).
  • Issues Ordinances when Parliament is not in session (Art. 123).

cards.front: What is the election procedure and eligibility criteria for any person to become governor of a state.
cards.back:
• Appointed by Pres. (Art 155) (on advice of CoM) President to consult concerned state CM(Convention based on Sarkaria and Punnchi)

 

  • Pre Appointment. (Qualifications) (Art 157)
    • Citizen + 35 Yrs
  • Post Appointment (Conditions) (Art 158)
    • Sitting MP/MLA can be appt., but will have torelinquish MP/MLA after winning
    • No other Office of Profit such as MP/MLA

cards.front: What are the constitutional discretionary powers of the Governor which are not available to the President?
cards.back:
• Reserving State Bills for President’s Assent(Article 200)
  • Recommending President’s Rule(Article 356)
  • Administrator of an adjoining Union Territory (additional charge)(Article 239)
  • Discretion in Sixth Schedule matters (Autonomous District Councils / royalty sharing)(Sixth Schedule)
  • Special responsibilities in certain States(Articles 371, 371A–371J)

cards.front: Mention situations where India behaves like a unitary system instead of a federal system.
cards.back:
• National Emergency
  • President’s Rule
  • Rajya Sabha resolution in national interest
  • Implementation of international treaties/agreements
  • Residuary legislative powers with Centre
  • All-India Services
  • Governor as Centre’s nominee
  • Single Constitution
  • Single Citizenship
  • Strong Centre in financial relations (taxation/grants/devolution)
Correct Answer : (d) 3 only

cards.front: Mention the circumstances under which an ordinary bill lapses upon dissolution of Lok Sabha.
cards.back:
An ordinary bill lapses on dissolution of the Lok Sabha if:

  1. It is pending in the Lok Sabha (whether introduced in Lok Sabha or transmitted from Rajya Sabha).
  2. It is passed by the Lok Sabha but pending in the Rajya Sabha.
  3. It is pending in the Lok Sabha and the President has notified a joint sitting, but the joint sitting has not yet taken place.

 

  • Does NOT lapse if it is pending in the Rajya Sabha only (and not passed by Lok Sabha yet).

cards.front:
What are the qualifications to be appointed as Governor of a State?
Also, what criteria were recommended by the Sarkaria Commission and the Punchhi Commission for the Governor’s post?
cards.back:
• Constitutional qualifications for Governor (India)
    • Must be a citizen of India. (Article 157)
    • Must have completed 35 years of age. (Article 157)
  • Punchhi Commission
    • Politically neutral, with proven integrity and administrative experience.
    • Not someone who has been actively involved in politics, particularly in the recent past.
  • Sarkaria Commission
    • A person of eminence in public life.
    • A person who is from outside the State (so that local politics doesn’t bias the office).
    • Appointment should be made after effective consultation with the Chief Minister of the State.

cards.front: In the District Planning Committee (DPC) and Metropolitan Planning Committee (MPC), what proportion of members must be elected and who elects them?
Explain the concept of constitutionalism.
cards.back:
• Constitutionalism = Idea that government power must be limited and controlled by a higher law (the Constitution) to protect rights and prevent arbitrariness.
  • It emphasises:
    • Limited Government – powers are defined and constrained.
    • Rule of Law – no one, including rulers, is above the law.
    • Separation of Powers & Checks and Balances – Legislature, Executive, Judiciary restrain each other.
    • Protection of Fundamental Rights – enforceable limits on the State.

cards.front: How are Gram Nyayalayas established and what is their jurisdiction?
cards.back:
Establishment

  • Established under the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008.
  • Set up by the State Government, in consultation with the High Court.
  • Established at the level of intermediate Panchayat (or a group of contiguous Panchayats)

Jurisdiction

1. Territorial jurisdiction

  • Over the area notified for the intermediate Panchayat / group of Panchayats.

2. Subject-matter jurisdiction

  • Criminal jurisdiction: Trial of specified minor offences (as notified/scheduled under the Act).
  • Civil jurisdiction: Matters such as property, money recovery, contracts, etc. of a limited nature/value, as notified under the Act.

cards.front:
With reference to the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) reaching its 100th anniversary, consider the following statements regarding its constitutional and financial status:

  1. The Commission was first established in 1926 as the Public Service Commission based on the recommendations of the Aitchison Commission.
  2. The expenses of the UPSC, including the salaries, allowances, and pensions of its members and staff, are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
  3. Under the Government of India Act, 1935, the Commission was renamed the Federal Public Service Commission and given a more expanded role compared to its 1926 predecessor.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

A) 1 and 2 only

B) 2 only

C) 2 and 3 only

D) 1, 2, and 3
cards.back:
Correct Answer: C) 2 and 3 only

 

  • Statement 1 is incorrect: While the Commission was indeed established on October 1, 1926, it was based on the recommendations of the Lee Commission (1924), not the Aitchison Commission (which dealt with civil services much earlier in 1886).Sir Ross Barker was its first Chairman.

  • Statement 2 is correct: Under Article 322, the entire administrative expenses of the UPSC are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. This means they are not subject to the annual vote of Parliament, which safeguards the Commission’s independence from political pressure.
  • Statement 3 is correct: The Government of India Act, 1935, transformed the body into the Federal Public Service Commission (FPSC) and also provided for the establishment of Provincial Public Service Commissions.

cards.front: Under what conditions can President’s Rule (Article 356) be imposed, what is its maximum duration for which it can remain enforced?
cards.back:
• Trigger (Art 356): When the President is satisfied that the Government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution.
    • Based on Governor’s report or otherwise.
    • Art 365 link: Failure to comply with Union directions can be treated as breakdown of constitutional machinery (basis for Art 356).
  • Duration + approvals:
    • Must be approved by both Houses within 2 months.
    • Once approved, valid for 6 months.
    • Can be extended every 6 months.
    • Maximum 3 years in total; beyond 1 year only if (i) National Emergency is in operation and (ii) EC certifies elections can’t be held.

Category of member When disqualified (lose membership)
Member elected on a party ticket (a) Voluntarily gives up membership of that party (even without formal resignation); OR (b) Votes/abstains contrary to party whip without prior permission and is not condoned by the party within the prescribed time
Independent member Joins any political party after being elected

cards.front: What is the maximum size of the Council of Ministers at the Centre and in the States? Which Constitutional Amendment introduced this limit?

  • Introduced by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003.

cards.front: What Provisions do Art. 31A, 31B and 31C contain. How do they provide supremacy to certain DPSP over Fundamental Rights.

cards.front: Explain the Purpose, Mode of Operation and Parliamentary control for consolidated fund of India, Public Account and Contingency fund of India.
What powers are vested in the Governor in Fifth Schedule Areas.
cards.back:
1. Can direct that a Parliament/State law shall NOT apply to a Scheduled Area or shall apply with modifications.
  2. Can make regulations for “peace and good government” of Scheduled Areas (commonly on land transfer, moneylending etc.; typically needs President’s assent).
  3. Sends reports to the President on administration of Scheduled Areas.
  4. Linked with Tribes Advisory Council (TAC) (advisory on tribal welfare).

cards.front: When can the President issue an ordinance? What are the key limitations?
cards.back:
• Can issue ordinance when:
    • Parliament is not in session and
    • Immediate action is necessary.
  • Limitations:
    • An ordinance has the same force as a law of Parliament, but
    • Must be laid before Parliament and ceases to operate at expiration of 6 weeks from reassembly, or earlier if disapproved.
    • It cannot be used to amend the Constitution.
    • Subject to judicial review; cannot be used for colourable legislation or repeated re-promulgation.

Answer the following questions related to Zonal Councils :

  1. How many Zonal Councils exist and under which Act were they established?
  2. Who presides over these councils and who are their members?
cards.back:
1. There are five Zonal Councils in India, established under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.
  2. Each Zonal Council is presided over by the Union Home Minister or a Minister nominated by the Union Government, and the Chief Ministers of the states in that zone are members. Union Ministers and Administrators of Union Territories may also participate.

cards.back: Correct Answer : (c) 2 and 3 only

cards.front:
Answer in True/False

  • The Basic Structure Doctrine is explicitly written in the Constitution.
  • Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, but not its Basic Structure.
  • Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights only if the amendment does not damage the Basic Structure.
  • The list of Basic Structure elements is exhaustive and fixed since 1973.
  • Judicial Review is part of the Basic Structure.
  • Minerva Mills (1980) upheld that Parliament’s amending power under Article 368 is unlimited.
cards.back:
1. False – The Basic Structure Doctrine is judicially evolved, not expressly mentioned in the Constitution.
  2. True – Kesavananda Bharati (1973) allowed amendments to all parts of the Constitution except the Basic Structure.
  3. True – Fundamental Rights can be amended only if the amendment does not destroy the Basic Structure.
  4. False – The Supreme Court has kept the Basic Structure list open-ended, not exhaustive.
  5. True – Judicial Review is essential to maintain constitutional supremacy and is part of the Basic Structure.
  6. False – Minerva Mills (1980) held that limited amending power itself is part of the Basic Structure.

cards.front: Explain the governance structure of the Union Territory of Delhi (NCT of Delhi) . Mention the role of the LG and Legislative Assembly.
cards.back:
• 69th Constitutional Amendment (1991): Inserted Article 239AA (and 239AB) and created:
    • a Legislative Assembly, and
    • a Council of Ministers headed by a Chief Minister.
  • Legislative power of Delhi Assembly: Can make laws on State List + Concurrent List matters except: Public Order, Police, Land.
  • Lieutenant Governor (LG): LG is the Administrator of NCTD; in subjects where Delhi Assembly can legislate
    •  has special powers to differ/ refer matters as per the constitutional scheme.

cards.front:
Consider the following statements about First-Past-The-Post (FPTP) and Proportional Representation (PR) systems:

  1. Under FPTP, the candidate who secures the highest number of votes in a constituency is declared elected, even if the votes polled are less than 50%.
  2. Under PR, seats are allocated to parties in proportion to their share of votes.
  3. In India, Lok Sabha elections follow the Proportional Representation system.
  4. In India, elections to the Rajya Sabha are conducted using Proportional Representation by means of the Single Transferable Vote (STV).

Which of the statements given above are correct?

(a) 1 and 2 only
(b) 1, 2 and 4 only
(c) 2 and 3 only
(d) 1, 3 and 4 only
cards.back: Answer: (b) 1, 2 and 4 only

cards.front: What is the procedure for the creation and abolition of a State Legislative Council? Currently, how many states have active Legislative Councils?
cards.back:
Procedure (Article 169, Constitution of India)

  • State Legislative Assembly Resolution:
    • The Legislative Assembly of the State must pass a resolution to create or abolish the Legislative Council.
    • The resolution must be passed by:
      • Majority of the total membership of the Assembly; and
      • Majority of not less than two-thirds of members present and voting.
  • Parliamentary Law:
    • After the Assembly resolution, Parliament may by law provide for the creation or abolition of the Council.
  • No Constitutional Amendment Requirement:
    • Such a law is not treated as a constitutional amendment under Article 368.
  • As of now, six (6) states in India have an active State Legislative Council:
    • Andhra Pradesh
    • Bihar
    • Karnataka
    • Maharashtra
    • Telangana
    • Uttar Pradesh

cards.front: What changes were made in Fundamental Rights by the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951?
cards.back:
• Article 19 – Freedom of Speech & Trade
    • Art. 19(1)(a) & 19(2):
      • Added new grounds for restricting speech:
        • Public order
        • Incitement to an offence
        • Friendly relations with foreign States
  • Art. 19(6):
    • Clarified State’s power to create monopolies in trade/business and impose “reasonable restrictions in public interest” on the freedom to practise any profession or carry on trade.
  • Article 15 – Special provisions
    • Inserted Art. 15(4):
    • Allowed the State to make special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs → constitutional backing for reservations.
  • Right to Property (then FR)
    • Inserted Articles 31A & 31B and Ninth Schedule
    • Protected agrarian reform/land reform laws from being struck down for violating FRs (esp. Art. 14, 19, 31).

cards.front:
Can the President:

  1. Return an ordinary Bill? 
  2. Return a Money Bill?
  3. Return a Constitutional Amendment Bill?
cards.back:
• Ordinary Bill:
    • Yes, can return once for reconsideration (Suspensive veto).
  • Money Bill:
    • Cannot return; only assent or withhold.
  • Constitutional Amendment Bill:
    • Must give assent; cannot withhold or return (only formal assent).

How is the Vice-President of India appointed/elected? Mention electoral college, system of election, and basic qualifications & tenure.
cards.back:
• Electoral College:
    • Elected + nominated members of both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha).
    • State MLAs are NOT part of this electoral college.
  • System:
    • Proportional representation by Single Transferable Vote (STV),
    • Secret ballot.
  • Qualifications:
    • Citizen of India,
    • ≥ 35 years,
    • Qualified for Rajya Sabha membership,
    • No office of profit under Union/State (exceptions: President, VP, Governor, Ministers).
  • Tenure:
    • 5 years, but can be re-elected any number of times; continues till successor assumes office.

cards.back:

cards.front:
"With reference to the Committee on Official Language:

  1. Under which Article of the Constitution is the Committee on Official Language constituted?
  2. Who constitutes this Committee and what is its composition?
  3. To whom does the Committee submit its recommendations?
cards.back:
1. The Committee on Official Language is constituted under Article 344(1) of the Indian Constitution.
  2. It is constituted by the President of India and consists of members representing the different languages specified in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution.
  3. The Committee submits its recommendations to the President of India, who then places them before both Houses of Parliament.

cards.front: Mention the ways the Lok Sabha Can Express Lack of Confidence
Explain the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 143 of the Constitution.
cards.back:
• Constitutional basis: Article 143
  • Authority invoking it: President of India
  • Categories of matters:
    • Question of law or fact of public importance (arisen or likely to arise)
    • Disputes arising from pre-Constitution treaties, agreements, covenants, sanads, etc., excluded from the Court’s original jurisdiction
  • Nature of Supreme Court’s response:
    • In the first category, the Court may give its opinion
    • In the second category, the Court must give its opinion
  • Nature of opinion: Advisory, not a judicial pronouncement. Not binding on the President, but 

    it facilitates the government to have an authoritative legal opinion on a matter to be decided by it.
Correct option: (d) 1, 2 and 3

cards.front: What is the main function of the Delimitation Commission (DC)? How is it appointed? Are its orders subject to judicial review?
cards.back:
• Main function:
    • To readjust/draw boundaries of Parliamentary (Lok Sabha) and State Assembly constituencies and (as applicable) determine/adjust reservation of seats for SC/ST based on population.
  • How appointed (set up):
    • Constituted by the Central Government under a Delimitation Act.
  • Typical composition:
    • Retired Supreme Court judge (Chairperson) + Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) + State Election Commissioner(s) (for the concerned states) as members.
  • Judicial review:
    • SC in Kishorchandra Chhanganlal Rathod case held that constitutional courts have the power to review orders of the Delimitation Commission if an order is manifestly arbitrary and irreconcilable to constitutional values.

cards.front: What is a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC)? How is it constituted and what does it do?
cards.back:
• Meaning: A Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) is an ad hoc (temporary) committee formed for a specific purpose usually to probe a specific issue/scam/policy matter or to scrutinise a particular bill.
  • Constitution: Created by a motion adopted by one House and agreed to by the other House (or by a joint motion).
  • Composition: Includes members from both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha; strength and party-wise representation are decided by Parliament.

Option d is the correct answer.

cards.front: From which act the CBI draws its power. Is it a statutaory body or not, and how is the CBI Director appointed?
cards.back:
• Legal basis / Act: CBI’s investigation powers flow from the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946.
  • Is it statutory?No. CBI was created by an executive resolution (1963), so it is not a statutory body (nor constitutional).
  • Director appointment: Appointed by the Central Government on recommendation of a committee:
    • Prime Minister (Chair)
    • Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha(or leader of largest opposition party if no LoP)
    • Chief Justice of India(or SC judge nominated by CJI)
    • Tenure:Minimum 2 years (can be extended up to 5 years total, in 1-year blocks).

cards.front: How can the Vice-President be removed from office?
List the exceptional circumstances under which the Centre can make laws on State List subjects.
cards.back:
The Centre can make laws on State subjects in the following situations:

  1. National Emergency (Art. 249): During an emergency
  2. Rajya Sabha Resolution (Art. 249): If 2/3rd members present & voting approve
  3. State Consent (Art. 252): When two or more states request Parliament
  4. Failure of Constitutional Machinery (Art. 356): President’s Rule in a state
  5. International Obligations (Art. 253): To implement treaties/agreements
  6. During Emergency (Art. 250): Parliament gets temporary power

cards.front: How is the Indian parliamentary system different from that of Britain (UK)?
Explain the meaning of terms associated with the word republic in the preamble.
cards.back:
• Sovereign
    • India is independent in internal & external matters; not subject to control of any external power.
    • Can freely decide on foreign policy, defence, economy, etc.
  • Socialist (added by 42nd CAA)
    • India follows democratic socialism → reduction of inequality, welfare state, not total state ownership.
    • Aims at social & economic justice.
  • Secular (added by 42nd CAA)
    • No State religion; State maintains neutrality toward all religions.
    • Equal protection and respect to all faiths.
  • Democratic
    • Popular sovereignty → government elected by people on the basis of universal adult franchise.
    • Political democracy: rule of law, equality of vote.
  • Republic
    • Elected, non-hereditary Head of State (President) with fixed tenure.
    • Public offices open to all citizens (subject to qualifications), not by birth.

cards.front: What changes were made by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act to Fundamental Rights, DPSP, and Fundamental Duties
cards.back:
• Fundamental Right (Part III)
    • Inserted Article 21A →
    • Made free and compulsory education for children 6–14 years a Fundamental Right.
  • Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV)
    • Amended Article 45 →
    • Earlier: free and compulsory education for all children up to 14 years.
    • Now: State shall provide early childhood care and education for all children below 6 years of age.
  • Fundamental Duties (Part IVA)
    • Amended Article 51A → inserted clause (k):
    • It is the duty of every parent/guardian to provide opportunities for education to their child/ward between 6 and 14 years.
